# Wasserstein GAN
The Wasserstein GAN (WGAN) is a variation of the Generative Adversarial Network designed to address instability issues in the original GAN framework, specifically the vanishing gradient problem and mode collapse. Unlike the standard GAN which relies on the Jensen-Shannon divergence and a sigmoid-activated discriminator, WGAN utilizes the Wasserstein distance (specifically the 1-Wasserstein metric) as the objective function. This metric is defined over a metric space and relies on the Kantorovich-Rubenstein duality, which allows for a more meaningful measure of distance between probability distributions, even when they have disjoint supports.
To ensure the discriminator (or "critic") function satisfies the Lipschitz constraint required by the Wasserstein distance, WGAN employs several training techniques. These include restricting the discriminator's output to be unbounded (removing the sigmoid), applying weight clipping to bound the Lipschitz norm of the network weights, and using spectral normalization to dynamically constrain the operator norm of the weight matrices. Additionally, the Gradient Penalty method can be used to enforce the Lipschitz condition by penalizing deviations in the gradient norm. By optimizing the objective $L_{WGAN}(\mu_G, D) = \mathbb{E} *{x \sim \mu_G}[D(x)] - \mathbb{E}* {x \sim \mu_{ref}}[D(x)]$, WGAN provides stable training dynamics and generates high-quality samples without the common failure modes of the vanilla GAN.
